prompt.context: Your client is a carpet manufacturer that sells to both commercial and residential customers. Their current production process is: (1) Buy dyed/pre-colored yarn, (2) Load yarn spools in a specific order onto machine, (3) Weave yarn into carpet, (4) Run carpet through carpet backing machine, (5) Cut, roll, and store the finished carpet. The client is considering investing in a new technology that will cost $25M (initial investment). With the new technology, the production process changes to: (1) Buy un-dyed yarn, (2) Spool yarn, (3) Weave yarn into carpet, (4) Dye carpet through a printing process, much like an inkjet printer, (5) Cut, roll, and store the finished carpet.
prompt.question: The client wants to know if they should invest in the new technology.

clarifying_info.q: Will the carpet made with the new technology be different in any way from the current product?
clarifying_info.a: We can assume that the new carpet will have a better texture and can therefore be sold at a higher-end offering.

framework: Assess impact on costs: yarn costs, ink costs, labor (spool loading), maintenance, electricity, training, warehousing
Assess impact on revenue: ability to sell higher-quality carpet at a price premium, potential to serve new market segments
Quantify cost savings per yard and total over machine useful life
Apply time-value-of-money to evaluate whether cost savings alone justify the $25M investment
Consider revenue upside: cannibalization of existing customers upgrading, plus new market capture
Calculate net incremental revenue (incremental gross revenue minus incremental production costs)
Provide recommendation with key risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What do you expect would be the likely impacts on costs from adopting the new technology?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify cost decreases (un-dyed yarn is cheaper, reduced labor on spool loading, lower warehousing due to make-to-order capability) and cost increases (ink costs, electricity, machine maintenance, training for new machine).

questions.prompt: We have aggregated the changes in costs, and it turns out we will save 25 cents per finished yard of carpet. How would you value the investment? (Data if asked: we produce 10M yards of finished carpet per year; machine has a 10-year useful life.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply savings per yard by annual volume to get annual savings, then multiply by useful life for a simple payback. Candidate should also flag time value of money, which means the undiscounted $25M total barely breaks even and does not account for maintenance or ink costs — signaling cost savings alone are insufficient to justify the investment.

math.setup: Annual savings = yards/year × savings/yard; Total savings = annual savings × useful life
steps: At face value this just breaks even, but time value of money means NPV of savings < $25M
Additionally, maintenance costs and ink costs are not yet captured in the $0.25 figure
math.answer: Simple payback is exactly 10 years (undiscounted); accounting for TVM, cost savings alone do not justify the investment.

questions.prompt: So what would you have to believe in order to justify this investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should articulate revenue-side arguments: ability to sell at a higher price point due to better texture, ability to win market share from competitors, ability to serve entirely new market segments, and increased flexibility by dyeing on demand rather than forecasting patterns in advance.

questions.prompt: It turns out we can sell the new, higher-quality carpet for $20/yard, which is a 25% premium over the standard carpet. We would still be able to produce and sell the standard carpet as well. What types of things would you think about in this scenario?
questions.guidance: Candidate should raise cannibalization of existing customers (some current buyers will upgrade, reducing standard carpet volumes) and new customer acquisition (the premium price unlocks a previously unreachable segment). The standard carpet price can be back-solved: $20 / 1.25 = $16/yard.

math.setup: Standard carpet price implied by 25% premium: $20 / 1.25

questions.prompt: We know that 30% of existing customers would upgrade to the new carpet, and there is a 70M yard/year market for higher-quality carpet that we couldn't sell to previously — we estimate we could capture 5% of that market. What would the incremental revenue be from selling the high-quality carpet?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate old revenue baseline, then new revenue under the two-product mix (remaining standard carpet sales + new high-quality carpet sales), and subtract to find incremental revenue.

math.setup: Old revenue = 10M yards × $16/yard. New mix: 70% of 10M = 7M yards standard at $16; upgraded existing = 30% of 10M = 3M yards new at $20; new market = 5% of 70M = 3.5M yards new at $20.
steps: New high-quality carpet sales total: (3M + 3.5M) = 6.5M yards × $20 = $130M

questions.prompt: Given this new information, what would you say about the NET incremental revenue from this machine? (Data if asked: cost per yard of original carpet = $10/yard; new carpet costs $9.75/yard after the $0.25 savings.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize that selling 3.5M more yards than before creates additional production costs. Net incremental revenue = incremental gross revenue minus incremental production costs. Strong candidates note that total volume increases from 10M to 13.5M yards, so new production costs must be computed for both the 7M standard yards and 6.5M new-carpet yards.

math.setup: Old production cost = 10M × $10. New production cost = 7M × $10 (standard) + 6.5M × $9.75 (new carpet, reflecting $0.25 saving). Net incremental cost = new cost − old cost. Net incremental revenue = incremental gross revenue − net incremental cost.

recommendation: Recommend proceeding with the $25M investment in the new dyeing technology

Cost savings alone ($2.5M/year undiscounted) barely break even over the machine's 10-year life when TVM is considered, but the revenue upside is compelling: net incremental revenue of $49M per year from the premium carpet opportunity
risks: Maintenance costs and ink costs could erode the $0.25/yard savings figure — these should be verified
Cannibalization could exceed the assumed 30% if more existing customers trade up
Market share capture in the 70M-yard premium segment may be harder to achieve than the 5% estimate
New technology introduces execution and operational risk during the transition
next_steps: Validate the $0.25/yard net cost savings figure by stress-testing ink cost and maintenance cost assumptions
Commission detailed market research on the addressable premium carpet segment and realistic share capture
Model NPV using a discount rate to confirm positive value even after TVM
Pilot the new technology at smaller scale before full $25M commitment if feasible
